narrative:
Chime (bc-chime, Bugcrowd managed, US neobank, $20K critical) was a clean triple-negative engagement: 0 verified secrets, 0 listable buckets, 0 confirmed takeover candidates across all three passes. The gh_org_supplement rule fired correctly — the bare `chime` GitHub org had only 3 repos, and suffix probing recovered `1debit` (47 public repos, Chime's corporate entity) as the proper Pass A target. Despite this, 0 secrets were found in either org (7+2 repos scanned), 0 code-search dork hits across 9 calls, and Pass C was not run. Chime's operational infrastructure is heavily private with no relevant public footprint beyond archived mobile dependencies and small Ruby gems.

The bucket pass ran 80 candidates through s3scanner, producing 10 flagged buckets — all 10 were `chime`-prefixed bare-stem variants (chime, chime-prod, chime-backup, chime-assets, chime-test, chime-production, chime-files, chime-logs, chime-dev, dev-chime). Every single one returned AccessDenied on the s3scanner_acl_recheck gate. This is the 12th consecutive engagement with a 100% s3scanner ACL false-positive rate, reinforcing that the recheck gate is permanent infrastructure, not a conservative hedge. Notably, none of the more distinctive brand variants (chimepayments, chimebank, saltlabs, 1debit) surfaced as s3scanner-flagged — squatter activity concentrates on the bare brand stem, not on program-distinctive names.

The most significant finding was a new false-positive class in the takeover pass: all 3 subzy VULNERABLE hits came from `email.*.chime.com` subdomains CNAME-ing to `mailgun.org`, and all 3 were disqualified by body recheck. The Uptimerobot fingerprint string (`page not found`) coincidentally matches Mailgun's edge which returns Go's `http.NotFound()` body verbatim — 19 bytes, `text/plain`, no Uptimerobot branding, and critically, CNAME target is `mailgun.org` not `stats.uptimerobot.com`. This is structurally identical to the Cargo Collective + SendGrid FP class documented in bc-seek: a short fingerprint string fires on a generic platform 404 served from a sender-authentication CNAME endpoint. The 3 same-engagement corroborations are enough for medium confidence. Mailgun sender-auth CNAMEs are account-bound (Mailgun requires domain ownership verification + API key binding), making them structurally not user-claimable just as SendGrid CNAMEs are.

A useful structural observation from the takeover pass: Chime uses Cloudflare as authoritative nameserver (leah.ns.cloudflare.com) but does NOT proxy service traffic through Cloudflare orange-cloud. Actual CNAME targets are CloudFront ARNs, awsglobalaccelerator.com, mailgun.org, and manage.microsoft.com — all direct. The existing `cdn.cloudflare.net` cname_hub_skip rule correctly fired 0 times on this engagement because the proxied Cloudflare pattern simply does not apply here. This confirms the rule is correctly scoped: Cloudflare-NS does not imply Cloudflare-proxied; only the orange-cloud/proxied case produces `*.cdn.cloudflare.net` CNAME chains. Generalizing the rule to catch all Cloudflare-NS customers would be wrong — those varied CNAME targets are exactly where takeover risk hides.

For revisits: run secrets Pass A on `1debit` only (skip bare `chime` org — 3 repos all accounted for); skip all `chime`-prefixed bucket variants in the scanner pass (all 10 returned AccessDenied, consistent with the bare-stem squatter pattern); the `mailgun.org` cname_hub_skip rule proposed here will eliminate the Uptimerobot FP class cleanly on future runs. SaltLabs (*.saltlabs.com) and ChimeSoftware remain unprobed GitHub orgs with 0 public repos each — no Pass A value there. If credentialed scanning ever becomes available, the `1debit` org's private repos are the highest-probability target for Chime's banking infrastructure secrets.
